sources.title: Carver-Washington Half Dollar
sources.type: official coin history and legislation summary

verifiedClaims.claim: Washington was born enslaved in Virginia in 1856; Tuskegee began in 1881 with 30 students and Washington led the school.
Carver joined Tuskegee in 1896, led its agriculture department, and spent 47 years there; his work included crop rotation and teaching farming methods.
Congress authorized the Washington half dollar in 1946 and amended the program in 1951 to include Carver; the combined coin was issued from 1951 through 1954.
The coin’s reverse is an outline map of the United States; the Mint calls it the last commemorative coin before the modern program began in 1982.

stats.statement: Washington’s biography and the 1881 Tuskegee school opening with 30 students.
Carver’s 1896 arrival at Tuskegee, 47-year tenure, agricultural teaching, and crop rotation work.

The paired commemorative half dollars were produced from 1951 through 1954; proceeds supported designated organizations, and the series was the last U.S. commemorative issue until the modern program began in 1982.
Booker T. Washington arrived in Tuskegee in June 1881; the school opened on July 4 with 30 students.
George Washington Carver joined Tuskegee's faculty in 1896 and spent 47 years there teaching agricultural science and promoting crop rotation to restore depleted soil.
The Mint identifies Isaac Scott Hathaway as the coin's designer; the obverse pairs Washington and Carver, and the reverse shows a map of the United States.
The Mint states that the coins were issued no later than August 7, 1954, and that proceeds went to named beneficiary organizations.
